comparisons.peer_topic: Noninterest expense increase drivers and prior year comparisons
comparisons.peer_summary: Noninterest expense increased $967 million to $66.8 billion in 2024 compared to 2023, primarily driven by higher revenue-related expenses and investments in people, operations, and technology, partially offset by higher FDIC expense in 2023 (including a $2.1 billion special assessment) and lower expenses from a liquidating business activity.
comparisons.comparison: Both MS and BAC report an increase in non-interest/noninterest expenses driven by compensation and revenue-related factors. MS attributes its 5% increase ($20.6B) primarily to formulaic payouts to representatives on higher compensable revenues (ms_2024_7_P068_S002). Similarly, BAC attributes its $967 million increase to $66.8B primarily to higher revenue-related expenses and investments in people (bac_2024_7_P017_S002). However, MS highlights lower non-compensation expenses like legal and professional services as an offset, whereas BAC highlights the absence of a massive $2.1 billion FDIC special assessment accrual from the prior year as a key comparative driver, noting its 2024 expenses were partially offset by this lower prior-year burden (bac_2024_7_P017_S002).

sentences.text: Non-interest expenses of $20,618 million in 2024 increased 5% compared with the prior year, as a result of higher Compensation and benefits expenses, partially offset by lower Non-compensation expenses.
• Compensation and benefits expenses increased, primarily due to an increase in the formulaic payout to Wealth Management representatives on higher compensable revenues.
Noninterest expense increased $967 million to $66.8 billion in 2024 compared to 2023.

The increase was primarily driven by higher revenue-related expenses as well as investments in people, operations and technology, partially offset by higher Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) expense in 2023, including $2.1 billion for the estimated special assessment amount arising from the closure of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank, and lower expenses related to a liquidating business activity.

comparisons.peer_topic: Factors driving 2024 operating expense decreases and increases
comparisons.peer_summary: Operating expenses decreased relative to 2023 due to lower commercial real estate impairments, GreenSky intangible asset write-downs, consumer platform goodwill impairments, and FDIC fees, partially offset by higher compensation and transaction-based expenses driven by improved performance. An additional $71 million FDIC special assessment fee was recognized in 2024.
comparisons.comparison: MS and GS both cite FDIC special assessment fees as a variable factor in their operating expense trends, but the direction and impact differ. MS reports lower FDIC special assessment costs in 2024 as part of decreased non-compensation expenses (ms_2024_7_P068_S003), contributing to its overall expense increase being smaller than the compensation growth. In contrast, GS explicitly recognizes an *incremental* $71 million expense for the FDIC special assessment fee in 2024 (gs_2024_7_P061_S003) due to updated estimates from SVB/Signature closures. Furthermore, while both mention higher compensation/benefits, MS’s overall expenses grew 5%, whereas GS’s operating expenses *decreased* 2% in 2024 due to massive prior-year impairments (CIEs, GreenSky) that did not recur, a structural difference in expense drivers not seen in MS's disclosure.

sentences.text: • Non-compensation expenses decreased, primarily driven by lower professional services and legal expenses and lower FDIC special assessment cost, partially offset by higher technology spend.
These decreases were partially offset by higher compensation and benefits expenses (reflecting improved operating performance) and higher transaction based expenses.

An incremental expense for the FDIC special assessment fee of $71 million was recognized in 2024, as the FDIC notified banks subject to the special assessment fee of the updated estimated cost to the Deposit Insurance Fund resulting from the closures in 2023 of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank.

comparisons.peer_summary: Noninterest expense was $91.8 billion, up 5%, driven by higher compensation and a $1.0 billion Visa share contribution to the foundation, partially offset by lower FDIC-related expenses due to the timing of special assessments.
comparisons.comparison: Both MS and JPM report a 5% increase in non-interest expenses, similarly driven by higher compensation tied to revenue performance. MS states compensation increased primarily due to formulaic payouts on higher compensable revenues (ms_2024_7_P068_S002). JPM states noninterest expense was up 5% driven by higher revenue-related compensation (jpm_2024_7_P018_S002). A key difference is the magnitude and nature of offsets: MS was offset by lower legal/professional services and FDIC costs (ms_2024_7_P068_S003), while JPM was offset by lower FDIC expenses (reflecting a $2.9B accrual in 2023 vs $725M in 2024) but significantly impacted by a one-time $1.0B Visa share contribution (jpm_2024_7_P018_S002), a specific item not present in MS's variance explanation.

sentences.text: Non-interest expenses of $20,618 million in 2024 increased 5% compared with the prior year, as a result of higher Compensation and benefits expenses, partially offset by lower Non-compensation expenses.
• Compensation and benefits expenses increased, primarily due to an increase in the formulaic payout to Wealth Management representatives on higher compensable revenues.
• Non-compensation expenses decreased, primarily driven by lower professional services and legal expenses and lower FDIC special assessment cost, partially offset by higher technology spend.

• Noninterest expense was $91.8 billion, up 5%, driven by higher compensation expense, including higher revenue-related compensation and growth in the number of employees, as well as a $1.0 billion contribution of Visa shares to the JPMorgan Chase Foundation recorded in the second quarter of 2024, partially offset by lower FDIC-related expense, reflecting a $2.9 billion special assessment recognized in the fourth quarter of 2023, compared with a $725 million increase to the FDIC special assessment recognized in the first quarter of 2024.
